statement: Across New York City community districts, more street trees per square kilometre go with a lower daytime summer surface temperature, after adjusting for poverty and percent Black residents.

graph_evidence.summary: Hasan et al. 2022 (Mymensingh, Bangladesh, Landsat 1988-2016): strong negative correlation of land surface temperature with NDVI. The graph stores r = -1.0, which is not the reported value (the abstract gives no number). The only vegetation-temperature finding found.

graph_evidence.relationship_id: (concepts I2CN3brExA tree, lHLIKbfnYp green space, RF7tCwCaa5 vegetation cover)
graph_evidence.summary: The tree concept has no relationships. Green space has 14, none with temperature, heat illness or emergency care. Surface temperature links only to air temperature (r about 0.9, 2 studies), population density (r 0.82) and deforestation (r 0.89). No finding connects trees or green space to heat-related ED visits.
Satellite surface temperature tracks ground air temperature (r about 0.9; R2 0.9).

literature.citation: Ziter CD, Pedersen EJ, Kucharik CJ, Turner MG. Scale-dependent interactions between tree canopy cover and impervious surfaces reduce daytime urban heat during summer. PNAS 2019;116:7575-7580.
literature.finding: Bicycle-transect air temperatures in Madison: daytime air temperature falls with canopy cover, nonlinearly, with the largest cooling above about 40% canopy at 60-90 m scales.

literature.citation: Madrigano J, Ito K, Johnson S, Kinney PL, Matte T. A case-only study of vulnerability to heat wave-related mortality in New York City (2000-2011). Environ Health Perspect 2015;123:672-678.
literature.finding: Heat-wave deaths in NYC were more likely among Black residents and in areas with less green space and higher surface temperature (case-only design).

prediction.magnitude: Per 1 SD of log street-tree density (2015 census, live trees per km2 of land), surface temperature lower by 0.5 to 3 F (Landsat, 17 July 2018). Unadjusted Pearson r between -0.2 and -0.7.
prediction.support_if: adjusted slope negative with upper 95% limit below 0
prediction.refute_if: adjusted slope positive with lower limit above 0

plan: Unit: 59 community districts. Exposure: 2015 Street Tree Census (uvpi-gqnh), count of status='Alive' by cb_num via SoQL group; land area of each CD from the NYC community district boundary file on NYC Open Data (shape_area, ft2 to km2). Secondary exposure: EHDP vegetative cover (indicator 2143, measure 690). Outcome: EHDP daytime summer surface temperature (indicator 2141, measure 688, CD). Covariates: percent in poverty and percent Black, averaged over NTAs within each CD from EHDP hvi-nta.csv. Model: OLS of surface temperature on z(log trees/km2), unadjusted and adjusted; HC3 SE. Secondary unit: NTA2010 (about 190), surface temperature and covariates from hvi-nta.csv, trees by the census nta field, NTA land area from the NTA 2010 boundary file.
alternatives: Building density and impervious cover drive both fewer street trees and hotter surfaces (dense Manhattan cores vs low-rise Staten Island)
Distance to water and parkland (parks are not street trees)
A single Landsat afternoon (17 July 2018) measures roofs and pavement, not air temperature at street level
